books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, B. The American System and Sectionalism
Henry Clay and the American System

stimulus.text:
| Part of the plan | What it would do |
|---|---|---|
| Protective tariff | Tax imported goods so American-made goods cost less |
| Second Bank of the United States | Steady the currency and lend credit for business |
| Internal improvements | Build roads and canals to link the regions |

Henry Clay of Kentucky called the three parts his American System. Congress chartered the Second Bank and passed a protective tariff in 1816.

stem: The American System’s results best show that regional interests

options.text: mattered less than party loyalty in every region of the country
options.misconception: The tariff and Bank fights split along regional lines, not party lines; region mattered most.

options.text: linked the North and Midwest together while leaving the South apart
disappeared once the Bank was chartered in 1816
options.misconception: Sectional fights grew after 1816, through the Missouri crisis, the tariffs, and nullification.

options.text: united all three regions behind the same program
options.misconception: The South opposed the tariff and the Bank; no program united all three regions.

rationales.A: Party loyalty did not decide the tariff fights. Northern and Southern members of the same party voted opposite ways, because their regions’ economies pointed opposite ways.
rationales.B: Canals and roads tied Northern factories to Midwestern farms, and migrants from the North settled the Midwest. The South, built on cotton and enslaved labor, was bypassed by those links and grew apart.
rationales.C: The Bank’s charter did not end sectional feeling. The Missouri crisis came in 1819, the tariff fights in the 1820s, and nullification in 1832.
rationales.D: The South fought the tariff as a tax on its shopping and fought the Bank as an Eastern power. A program one region calls robbery does not unite anyone.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the System built. Roads and canals linked Northern mills to Midwestern farms.
2. Ask who was left out. The South’s cotton economy ran on rivers and sea, not on the new Northern links.
3. Ask what the South did. It opposed the tariff and the Bank, and the opposition hardened into nullification.
4. Put it together. One plan linked two regions and pushed the third away.
Background: the books note that roads and railroads connected the North and the Midwest but tended to bypass the South, and migration tied the North to the Midwest culturally.
Remember: a national plan can link some regions by leaving another out.
